content.title: An engineering of existing components
content.review:
Overall summary: 
The authors of this manuscript propose to use the idea of dynamic routing between capsules, originally for image classification, to learn node embedding in graph data for node classification. The method was tested on six relational data sets.

Clarity: 
I am not convened that the dynamic routing between capsules for graph has similar implication as in computer vision. It is claimed that the CapsG model can preserve relative positions of nodes, but I believe it is straightforward to obtain the relative positions of nodes from just observing the graph structure. Why random walk is used? Is it necessary? Can the context nodes simply be defined within the Markov blanket of the target node? Furthermore, it is not mentioned in the manuscript how to compute the u_i vectors when feature vectors are not given. 

Originality: 
It is an extended work based on recent development of node embedding. Basically, it is a combination of random walk based methods and Hinton's first capsule net. Therefore, the originality of this work is not strong.

Significance: 
The results obtained on six data sets are not impressive. Due to marginal gain in means and large variations on some data sets, it is difficult to say that the proposed method is significantly better than existing ones. Moreover, the authors mentioned that test nodes were removed when training in an inductive fashion. Were the validation nodes removed as well?
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Thank you for your comments
content.comment:
We would like to thank you for your comments.

For some clarifications:

a. We use the random walk strategy to have more contexts at many hops away,  this helps to infer the better embeddings for the unseen nodes whose neighbors are also unseen in the inductive setting. Note that other approaches such as GAT, GCN encounter the problem for these cases.

b. We mentioned in the first paragraph of page 3, when feature vectors are not given, x_i is randomly initialized and updated during training.

c. We follow the identical experimental setups used in the NIPS2017 paper "Learning graph representations with embedding propagation" for both transductive and inductive settings. In the inductive setting, only the test nodes are removed, as mentioned in the ICML2016 paper "Revisiting Semi-Supervised Learning with Graph Embeddings".

d. Our unsupervised CapsG significantly outperforms the semi-supervised models such as GCN, GAT on Cora, CiteSeer and Pubmed in the inductive setting.

display_title: decent novelty but motivations and approaches not convincing enough

content.title: decent novelty but motivations and approaches not convincing enough
content.review:
To solve the problem fo “preserving relative positions of nodes”, the paper applied the capsule network to the graph node embedding task and proposed the model named “CapsG”. The CapsG construct two capsule layers and utilize the dynamic routing between capsules to iteratively update the target node representation in a random walk. The experimental results on datasets with node features and without node features both seem promising. I think the idea of the model is interesting, but I have some concerns about the motivation and the soundness of the model.

1. I am not convinced of the motivation of “preserving the relative positions of nodes”. The authors claimed in the Introduction that the CNN has the problem of preserving the relative positions, and the problem of GCN based models are just because they used “the variant of CNNs”. To me the GNNs, even the GCN based models have very different mechanisms from CNNs, this simple inference is not convincing at all. I would like to see more detailed example or explanation about how GCNs encounter this problem. In fact, many graph node embedding models, such as Deepwalk, node2vec or GAT seem not to have this problem to me.

2. I enjoyed the section “Comparing CapsG with related works”, but after reading that section I had a strong feeling that using capsule layers may not be necessary in this model, or at least not a very natural selection. One question is about the definition of the capsule layers. The approach used the capsule layers for each random walk, where the capsules in the first capsule layer are just single nodes. It is essentially just an extension to the node aggregation mechanism by using multi-hop node information. Another question is about “W_i” in Eq. (1). It is an important parameter which defines the transformation for each capsule. And it is one of the major differences from other models such as GAT. However, The index of capsules are randomly decided and different indices will result in different output vectors, which seems to conflict with the motivation of position invariance.

3. For experiments, I think it is better to demonstrate the advantages by adding two results: the ablation model using the same “W_i” for different capsules in Eq. (1); the running time of CapsG. As it samples a number of random walks for each node, and update target node representation in each random walk with many iterations, I am curious whether it slows down compared to other GNNs.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Limited technical contribution and evaluation part needs improvement
content.review:
This paper applies the idea of dynamic routing between capsules to network embedding application and achieves comparable results as baseline methods. 

Strength:
1)	It is interesting to explore how ‘dynamic routing between capsules’ performs on the task of network embedding.
Weakness:
1)	It does not seem to be much technical challenge to apply the capsule idea to network embedding. So technical contribution of this paper is limited.
2)	The paper claims by preserving relative positions of nodes, it is able to solve the problem of losing potential information. It could be helpful if the author make it clear why preserving relative positions of nodes is important for network embedding.

3) Evaluation:
a. For the three datasets with node features are of the same type: citation networks. The experimental results could be more convincing if the paper could use other type of attributed networks.
b. The paper does not mention how the parameters for baseline methods (e.g., LINE, node2vec) are set.
c. The baseline methods used in Table 3 is a bit too old. The most recent baseline used for the transductive setting was proposed in 2016 (node2vec). Network embedding is a field that grows very rapidly, and many new approaches are proposed in the past two years. The author should consider include more recent methods as baselines in Table 3.

Overall, I think this paper is below the borderline of acceptance, since the technical contribution of this paper is a bit limited, and the evaluation result is relatively weak.

content.title: Some clarifications!
content.comment:
We would like thank you for your comments.

We would like to clarify our evaluation to your #3:

a. Most published papers on the node classification task rely on Cora, Citeseer and Pubmed, and this is same for some ICLR2019 submissions. Thus, we do not have a plan to work on other datasets of attributed networks.

b. We follow the identical experimental setups used in the NIPS2017 paper "Learning graph representations with embedding propagation" for both transductive and inductive settings . So we refer to the same baselines as mentioned in this NIPS2017  paper. 

c. We guess you mentioned to Table 2, not Table 3. In Table 2, we refer to the NIPS2017 paper having the enthusiastic experimental setups, thus the results of the baselines are considerable to use for a comparison.

In Table 3, we provide you up-to-date results on the node classification task for the transductive and inductive settings. In particular, our unsupervised CapsG outperforms the semi-supervised models such as GCN, GAT on Cora, CiteSeer and Pubmed in the inductive setting where we follow the standard setups used in the NIPS2017 paper and the ICML2016 paper "Revisiting Semi-Supervised Learning with Graph Embeddings".
